ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was assessed as minimal risk and approved by the University of St Andrews Teaching and Research Ethics Committee (UTREC; approval reference PS-1485-2292-2026).
Across five experiments, participants were exposed to business-related objects (e.g., briefcases) during an ostensibly unrelated task.
table.header: Introduction Priming, Objects, and Social Meaning

table.text: Thirty participants were recruited using opportunity sampling from the University of St Andrews community.

Two participants were subsequently excluded during data screening, leaving a final analysed sample of N = 28 (see Data Handling and Exclusions); because data were anonymised at collection, the demographic characteristics reported here describe the full recruited sample.
Participants were recruited using opportunity sampling via university email circulars, online noticeboards, and printed posters distributed across the University of St Andrews campus.

Exclusion criteria were specified as follows and participant data were excluded if any of the criteria applied: (a) failure of the comprehension-check following the task instructions; (b) total task completion time falling more than 50% below or above the sample mean, indicating either rushed non-engagement or interrupted responding, following duration-based screening practice for computer-administered tasks (Meade & Craig, 2012); (c) identical responses on ≥ 50% of consecutive trustworthiness ratings, indicating straight-lining (see Maniaci & Rogge, 2014; Meade & Craig, 2012); (d) failure on two or more of the three embedded attention-check items; or (e) a non-response rate exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials, which would reduce the percondition trial count below the 10-trial minimum specified in the a priori power analysis (see above).

table.text: Each participant completed one of three Gorilla spreadsheets (i.e., trial structures), which intermixed the trust, filler, and catch trials, while the three attention checks were held at fixed positions across all versions to maintain an even spread throughout the experiment.

Following the tutorial, participants completed a short comprehension check confirming that they understood the task instructions and the use of the slider; failure to answer all items correctly met exclusion criterion (a).

Two participants were excluded for non-response exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials (31.1% and 64.4% missing respectively) as per exclusion criteria (e); no other exclusion criteria (a-d) were met, leaving a final analytic sample of N = 28 and 1,217 valid trustworthiness-rating trials (Novel n = 410, Home n = 403, and Work n = 404) across all participants.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Across five experiments, participants were exposed to business-related objects (e.g., briefcases) during an ostensibly unrelated task.

> Thirty participants were recruited using opportunity sampling from the University of St Andrews community.

> Two participants were subsequently excluded during data screening, leaving a final analysed sample of N = 28 (see Data Handling and Exclusions); because data were anonymised at collection, the demographic characteristics reported here describe the full recruited sample.

> Participants were recruited using opportunity sampling via university email circulars, online noticeboards, and printed posters distributed across the University of St Andrews campus.

> Exclusion criteria were specified as follows and participant data were excluded if any of the criteria applied: (a) failure of the comprehension-check following the task instructions; (b) total task completion time falling more than 50% below or above the sample mean, indicating either rushed non-engagement or interrupted responding, following duration-based screening practice for computer-administered tasks (Meade & Craig, 2012); (c) identical responses on ≥ 50% of consecutive trustworthiness ratings, indicating straight-lining (see Maniaci & Rogge, 2014; Meade & Craig, 2012); (d) failure on two or more of the three embedded attention-check items; or (e) a non-response rate exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials, which would reduce the percondition trial count below the 10-trial minimum specified in the a priori power analysis (see above).

> Each participant completed one of three Gorilla spreadsheets (i.e., trial structures), which intermixed the trust, filler, and catch trials, while the three attention checks were held at fixed positions across all versions to maintain an even spread throughout the experiment.

> Following the tutorial, participants completed a short comprehension check confirming that they understood the task instructions and the use of the slider; failure to answer all items correctly met exclusion criterion (a).

> Two participants were excluded for non-response exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials (31.1% and 64.4% missing respectively) as per exclusion criteria (e); no other exclusion criteria (a-d) were met, leaving a final analytic sample of N = 28 and 1,217 valid trustworthiness-rating trials (Novel n = 410, Home n = 403, and Work n = 404) across all participants.

> Participants were grouped by their differences in Home and Work affiliation ratings, classifying participants as Home-leaning (Home > Work by more than 20 points), Work-leaning (Work > Home by more than 20 points), or Balanced (all remaining participants).

> However, the Home prime interaction was sensitive to how affiliation was specified and weakened to non-significance when the five Home-leaning participants were instead compared against all other participants combined (i.e., Work-leaning and Balanced; b = 4.93, p = .062).

> These participants were nevertheless retained, as autism was not an exclusion criterion.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A simulation-based a priori power analysis was conducted using the simr package (Version 1.0.9; Green & MacLeod, 2016) in R (Version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026), following recommendations for linear mixed models (LMM; Kumle et al., 2021; Meteyard & Davies, 2020). A dataset was simulated to reflect a one-way within-subjects design with three condition categories (Home, Work, Novel), each providing 10 trials per condition (840 total observations) for a presumed sample of 28 participants. The final design included 15 trials per condition; the lower simulated trial count of 10 therefore provided a conservative estimate that accounted for potential trial losses, as participants could skip trials during the experiment. A small-to-medium effect size was specified (β = 3; f = 0.15), below Kay et al.'s (2004) reported effects (partial η² = 0.13 to 0.32; f = 0.39 to 0.69). This conservative estimate is motivated by two considerations: the shift in the dependent variable from competition to trustworthiness, which may attenuate effects (Cesario, 2014), and broader cautions against overestimating reported priming effects (McCarthy et al., 2018; Open Science Collaboration, 2015). Random intercepts were specified for participants (ICC = .220)foot_0, with a residual standard deviation of σ = 13 and a grand mean of 48 assumed. Based on 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations of the specified model parameters (seed = 2025 for reproducibility, powerSim, α = 0.05), the analysis returned 81.90% power (95% CI [79.37, 84.24]) at 28 participants. The power curve indicated that 80% was reached between 25 and 28 participants. Therefore, a recruitment target of 30 participants was set to increase power further and allow for potential participant exclusions.

There was also no evidence that any prime effect was concentrated among face-types. Neither prime interacted with normative face-trustworthiness level, nor face ambiguity, where the lack of contextual information was expected to exert greater influence on the judgement (Cesario, 2014; Loersch & Payne, 2011). At the same time, normative facial trustworthiness strongly predicted participants' trust ratings (b = 4.61, p < .001), indicating that the measure was sensitive to the judgement being made. This, together with evidence that trustworthiness judgements of such faces are susceptible to task-relevant priming (Posten et al., 2014), provides little indication that the null finding resulted from an insensitive measure or a paradigm inherently incapable of priming. The study was also powered to detect effects smaller than those typically reported within the incidental priming literature (e.g., DeCoster & Claypool, 2004; Kay et al., 2004; Weingarten et al., 2016), although smaller effects remain possible.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was assessed as minimal risk and approved by the University of St Andrews Teaching and Research Ethics Committee (UTREC; approval reference PS-1485-2292-2026).
live_data_statements: Across five experiments, participants were exposed to business-related objects (e.g., briefcases) during an ostensibly unrelated task.
Thirty participants were recruited using opportunity sampling from the University of St Andrews community.

Two participants were subsequently excluded during data screening, leaving a final analysed sample of N = 28 (see Data Handling and Exclusions); because data were anonymised at collection, the demographic characteristics reported here describe the full recruited sample.
Participants were recruited using opportunity sampling via university email circulars, online noticeboards, and printed posters distributed across the University of St Andrews campus.

Exclusion criteria were specified as follows and participant data were excluded if any of the criteria applied: (a) failure of the comprehension-check following the task instructions; (b) total task completion time falling more than 50% below or above the sample mean, indicating either rushed non-engagement or interrupted responding, following duration-based screening practice for computer-administered tasks (Meade & Craig, 2012); (c) identical responses on ≥ 50% of consecutive trustworthiness ratings, indicating straight-lining (see Maniaci & Rogge, 2014; Meade & Craig, 2012); (d) failure on two or more of the three embedded attention-check items; or (e) a non-response rate exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials, which would reduce the percondition trial count below the 10-trial minimum specified in the a priori power analysis (see above).

Each participant completed one of three Gorilla spreadsheets (i.e., trial structures), which intermixed the trust, filler, and catch trials, while the three attention checks were held at fixed positions across all versions to maintain an even spread throughout the experiment.

Following the tutorial, participants completed a short comprehension check confirming that they understood the task instructions and the use of the slider; failure to answer all items correctly met exclusion criterion (a).

Two participants were excluded for non-response exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials (31.1% and 64.4% missing respectively) as per exclusion criteria (e); no other exclusion criteria (a-d) were met, leaving a final analytic sample of N = 28 and 1,217 valid trustworthiness-rating trials (Novel n = 410, Home n = 403, and Work n = 404) across all participants.

Participants were grouped by their differences in Home and Work affiliation ratings, classifying participants as Home-leaning (Home > Work by more than 20 points), Work-leaning (Work > Home by more than 20 points), or Balanced (all remaining participants).

However, the Home prime interaction was sensitive to how affiliation was specified and weakened to non-significance when the five Home-leaning participants were instead compared against all other participants combined (i.e., Work-leaning and Balanced; b = 4.93, p = .062).
These participants were nevertheless retained, as autism was not an exclusion criterion.

info.title: Object-Based Priming and the Perceived Trustworthiness of Unfamiliar Faces: A Test of Home and Work Primes

text.text: Briefly viewing everyday home or work objects did not reliably change how trustworthy unfamiliar faces appeared.
Both categories produced small, similar, non-significant increases relative to novel objects, rather than the predicted opposing effects.
Any influence of object meaning on trustworthiness judgements is likely to be small.
The proposition that incidental cues can influence social judgements and behaviour has a longstanding presence in psychological research (Bargh & Chartrand, 1999; Loersch & Payne, 2011).
text.formatted: The proposition that incidental cues can influence social judgements and behaviour has a longstanding presence in psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bargh & Chartrand, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In an early demonstration, Berkowitz and LePage (1967) found that previously provoked participants behaved more aggressively towards a confederate when a weapon was visible in the testing room, an effect attributed to the aggressive associations the weapon carried into an otherwise unrelated situation.
text.formatted: In an early demonstration, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Berkowitz and LePage (1967)</ref> found that previously provoked participants behaved more aggressively towards a confederate when a weapon was visible in the testing room, an effect attributed to the aggressive associations the weapon carried into an otherwise unrelated situation.

text.text: However, the reliability of such object-based effects soon came under debate, as replications often produced weaker and less consistent findings than originally reported (e.g., Page & Scheidt, 1971; Turner & Simons, 1974).
text.formatted: However, the reliability of such object-based effects soon came under debate, as replications often produced weaker and less consistent findings than originally reported (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Page & Scheidt, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Turner & Simons, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: Partly for this reason, subsequent work came to favour word-based primes, which offered greater control over the concepts activated, particularly for less direct associations where a single object could evoke several meanings (Bargh & Chartrand, 2000; Higgins, 1996).
text.formatted: Partly for this reason, subsequent work came to favour word-based primes, which offered greater control over the concepts activated, particularly for less direct associations where a single object could evoke several meanings <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bargh & Chartrand, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Higgins, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Research using word-based primes later demonstrated how this activation could bias interpersonal judgements.

For example, Higgins et al. (1977) exposed participants to trait words such as reckless or adventurous as part of an ostensibly unrelated perceptual task, before they read information about a target person whose behaviour was open to either interpretation.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Higgins et al. (1977)</ref> exposed participants to trait words such as reckless or adventurous as part of an ostensibly unrelated perceptual task, before they read information about a target person whose behaviour was open to either interpretation.

text.text: Participants later judged the same ambiguous behaviour as reckless or as adventurous depending on which words they had previously encountered. Srull and Wyer (1979) showed that this assimilation grew stronger the more frequently and recently the trait category had been activated, tying the effect to the momentary accessibility of the primed concept rather than to any independently motivated inferences about the target.
text.formatted: Participants later judged the same ambiguous behaviour as reckless or as adventurous depending on which words they had previously encountered. <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Srull and Wyer (1979)</ref> showed that this assimilation grew stronger the more frequently and recently the trait category had been activated, tying the effect to the momentary accessibility of the primed concept rather than to any independently motivated inferences about the target.

text.text: Together, these findings show that incidentally activated concepts can bias interpersonal judgement; the key question is whether object-derived concepts can do the same.

Although psychology has given comparatively little attention to whether discrete objects can act as primes, the broader social sciences, particularly consumer research, have long regarded objects and everyday physical settings as important influences on how people are perceived and judged (Solway et al., 2016).

text.text: Within this literature, Kotler's (1973) foundational theory of atmospherics proposed that environmental features such as lighting, sound, and room layout communicate socially relevant information about a setting, including the behavioural norms associated with it.
text.formatted: Within this literature, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Kotler's (1973)</ref> foundational theory of atmospherics proposed that environmental features such as lighting, sound, and room layout communicate socially relevant information about a setting, including the behavioural norms associated with it.

text.text: Subsequent research supported this proposition, showing that atmospheric cues can systematically influence behaviour and evaluative judgements, including impulse purchasing (Mohan et al., 2013) and perceptions of service quality (Baker et al., 1994; also see Bitner, 1992; Turley & Milliman, 2000).
text.formatted: Subsequent research supported this proposition, showing that atmospheric cues can systematically influence behaviour and evaluative judgements, including impulse purchasing <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Mohan et al., 2013)</ref> and perceptions of service quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 1994</ref>; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bitner, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Turley & Milliman, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, this logic extends from whole settings to individual objects: Schuldt et al. (2012), for example, demonstrated that manipulating an object's visual angle alone, such as presenting an SUV head-on rather than in profile, was sufficient to alter observers' ratings of a target owner on status-and power-related traits.
text.formatted: Crucially, this logic extends from whole settings to individual objects: <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Schuldt et al. (2012)</ref>, for example, demonstrated that manipulating an object's visual angle alone, such as presenting an SUV head-on rather than in profile, was sufficient to alter observers' ratings of a target owner on status-and power-related traits.

text.text: Collectively, these findings suggest that object-based cues can influence interpersonal evaluations, but only when the object's meaning maps fairly directly onto the trait being judged.
Therefore, the current question is whether an object's category membership can carry meaning across into a judgement it has no direct bearing on.
One account of how objects come to hold such meaning comes from research in material culture, an interdisciplinary field spanning anthropology, sociology, and archaeology.

This research has consistently shown that particular objects are associated with specific social settings and can convey the normative expectations of those environments, rather than any meaning intrinsic to the objects themselves (Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981; Dant, 1999).
text.formatted: This research has consistently shown that particular objects are associated with specific social settings and can convey the normative expectations of those environments, rather than any meaning intrinsic to the objects themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Dant, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, objects may function as cues that activate the broader social schemas associated with their usual environments.

For example, home-related objects are frequently associated with intimacy, familiarity, and care (Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981; Rochberg-Halton, 1984), characteristics that closely align with trust (Dupuis & Thorns, 1998; Miller, 1997).
text.formatted: For example, home-related objects are frequently associated with intimacy, familiarity, and care <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Rochberg-Halton, 1984)</ref>, characteristics that closely align with trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Dupuis & Thorns, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Miller, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, work-or office-related objects are more frequently associated with hierarchy, formality, and instrumental purpose (Fiske, 1991; Hodder, 2012; Nippert-Eng, 1996), characteristics of the formal, contractual interactions associated with reduced trust (Malhotra & Murnighan, 2002; Sitkin & Roth, 1993).
text.formatted: By contrast, work-or office-related objects are more frequently associated with hierarchy, formality, and instrumental purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Fiske, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Hodder, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Nippert-Eng, 1996)</ref>, characteristics of the formal, contractual interactions associated with reduced trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Malhotra & Murnighan, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Sitkin & Roth, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: These contrasting associations suggest that home-and work-related objects may have the potential to differentially influence trust-related judgements, providing a useful test of whether objectderived social meaning influences social perceptions.
Yet whether such objects systematically influence trustworthiness judgements remains largely untested.
Establishing whether these associations shift trust judgements first requires specifying the mechanism by which an object might activate them.

Within psychology, the most established framework for understanding how associated concepts become accessible is semantic priming, whereby a stimulus is easier to process when it follows a meaningfully related cue, as when bread is preceded by butter rather than an unrelated word (Meyer & Schvaneveldt, 1971).
text.formatted: Within psychology, the most established framework for understanding how associated concepts become accessible is semantic priming, whereby a stimulus is easier to process when it follows a meaningfully related cue, as when bread is preceded by butter rather than an unrelated word <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Meyer & Schvaneveldt, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Such facilitation does not require two concepts to be learned through association or co-occurrence (e.g., nurse and doctor); it can also arise when a prime and a target share meaning, features, or category membership irrespective of a learned grouping (e.g., whale and dolphin; Hutchison, 2003; McRae & Boisvert, 1998).
text.formatted: Such facilitation does not require two concepts to be learned through association or co-occurrence (e.g., nurse and doctor); it can also arise when a prime and a target share meaning, features, or category membership irrespective of a learned grouping (e.g., whale and dolphin; <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Hutchison, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">McRae & Boisvert, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is relevant to the present study, as the objects used here (e.g., an ironing board or a teapot) are linked less by habitual co-occurrence than by their shared membership to a broader, potentially unlearned environmental category (i.e., the home).
It is this category-based form of semantic relatedness and the social meaning attached to the category that the present manipulation depends on.
Classical network models of semantic memory explain how such relationships influence subsequent processing.

These models represent concepts as nodes within a network connected by weighted links, so that activating one concept simultaneously raises the accessibility of those related to it (Collins & Loftus, 1975).
text.formatted: These models represent concepts as nodes within a network connected by weighted links, so that activating one concept simultaneously raises the accessibility of those related to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Collins & Loftus, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: This heightened accessibility, termed constructaccessibility, biases the interpretation of ambiguous targets towards the activated construct when that construct is relevant to the judgement being made (Higgins et al., 1977; Srull & Wyer, 1979).
text.formatted: This heightened accessibility, termed constructaccessibility, biases the interpretation of ambiguous targets towards the activated construct when that construct is relevant to the judgement being made <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Higgins et al., 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Srull & Wyer, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Such effects are strongest when information about the target is limited, so that the accessible construct, rather than the target itself, guides interpretation.

Their direction, however, depends on the strength of the prime: moderate primes are assimilated into the judgement, whereas highly salient or extreme primes serve as a comparison standard, producing contrast and thereby shifting the judgement away from the primed construct (Herr, 1986).
text.formatted: Their direction, however, depends on the strength of the prime: moderate primes are assimilated into the judgement, whereas highly salient or extreme primes serve as a comparison standard, producing contrast and thereby shifting the judgement away from the primed construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Herr, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, because the everyday objects (home and work) used here are moderate rather than extreme primes, assimilation is predicted.

The conditions under which such accessibility affects subsequent judgements are specified by the situated inference model, which proposes that priming only arises when accessible content is misattributed to the perceiver's own response to the target and incorporated into its interpretation.

On this account, the effect is strongest when the content is readily accessible and consistent with the perceiver's existing attitudes towards the primed category, and weaker when the prime is sufficiently salient to be recognised as an external cue rather than as part of the perceiver's own reaction (Loersch & Payne, 2011).
text.formatted: On this account, the effect is strongest when the content is readily accessible and consistent with the perceiver's existing attitudes towards the primed category, and weaker when the prime is sufficiently salient to be recognised as an external cue rather than as part of the perceiver's own reaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The same object-based prime may therefore affect one perceiver and not another, contingent on each perceiver's context-specific association with it.
Together, these two accounts explain how the social meaning of an object category could shift judgements of an ambiguous target and why that shift may vary from person to person.
A further question is whether these semantic processes are specific to words or extend to object images.

Neurophysiological evidence indicates that they are not confined to words: the N400, an event-related potential that indexes the ease of integrating a stimulus into a semantic context, is elicited comparably by words and object images (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Lau et al., 2008; Salisbury, 2004; Willems et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Neurophysiological evidence indicates that they are not confined to words: the N400, an event-related potential that indexes the ease of integrating a stimulus into a semantic context, is elicited comparably by words and object images <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kutas & Federmeier, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Lau et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Salisbury, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Willems et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This cross-format equivalence is consistent with a partially overlapping, transmodal semantic system, in which concepts are represented across modalities rather than tied to a single verbal format (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017), supporting the extension of predominantly word-based priming accounts to object-based primes.
text.formatted: This cross-format equivalence is consistent with a partially overlapping, transmodal semantic system, in which concepts are represented across modalities rather than tied to a single verbal format <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Lambon Ralph et al., 2017)</ref>, supporting the extension of predominantly word-based priming accounts to object-based primes.

text.text: The timing of a prime also matters.

Although no single theory captures the full range of semantic priming effects (Neely, 1991), a prominent account, two-process theory, distinguishes between two mechanisms that operate over different temporal intervals (Neely, 1977a (Neely, , 1991)).
text.formatted: Although no single theory captures the full range of semantic priming effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Neely, 1991)</ref>, a prominent account, two-process theory, distinguishes between two mechanisms that operate over different temporal intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Neely, 1977a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Neely, , 1991))</ref>.

text.text: The first, spreading activation, is a fast, automatic, bottom-up process.
It briefly raises the accessibility of closely related or over-learned concepts before decaying within a few hundred milliseconds.
It is therefore most readily observed at short prime-to-target intervals (Neely, 1977b; Neely et al., 2010).
text.formatted: It is therefore most readily observed at short prime-to-target intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Neely, 1977b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Neely et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The second, controlled processing, is a slower, strategic, top-down process in which a prime is used to generate expectations about a subsequent target.

This process can apply semantic relationships more flexibly, extending activation to less closely associated concepts when sufficient time is available to redirect attention (Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2005; Neely, 1977b; Posner & Snyder, 1975).
text.formatted: This process can apply semantic relationships more flexibly, extending activation to less closely associated concepts when sufficient time is available to redirect attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Neely, 1977b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Posner & Snyder, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is particularly relevant to the present study, as the proposed association between an object and a social category is cross-domain and therefore less likely to arise through automatic spreading activation.
Consequently, the present design favours the controlled-processing account (see Design Rationale).
With the mechanism specified, the question becomes whether object categories have been shown to activate social concepts in this way.
Evidence that object categories can produce cross-domain social activation comes from Kay et al. (2004).
text.formatted: Evidence that object categories can produce cross-domain social activation comes from <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kay et al. (2004)</ref>.

text.text: Across five experiments, participants were exposed to business-related objects (e.g., briefcases) during an ostensibly unrelated task.

This exposure increased the accessibility of competition-related concepts, biased ambiguous social interactions towards more competitive interpretations, and shifted offers in an economic bargaining game towards greater self-interest, even though the objects bore no relation to the subsequent tasks.
These findings suggest that an object's membership within a coherent environmental category can activate associated social concepts, which can influence subsequent social judgements and behaviour.

Importantly, their fifth experiment showed that this effect emerged only when the situation was ambiguous, indicating that the activated concept shaped how an underspecified situation was interpreted rather than producing a fixed response. Neuberg (1988) reported a related pattern using subliminal competition-related word primes, wherein competitively predisposed participants played more competitively towards a partner, but only once the partner had made a move that could be interpreted, suggesting that the prime biased how participants construed their partner's behaviour rather than altering their behaviour directly.
text.formatted: Importantly, their fifth experiment showed that this effect emerged only when the situation was ambiguous, indicating that the activated concept shaped how an underspecified situation was interpreted rather than producing a fixed response. <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Neuberg (1988)</ref> reported a related pattern using subliminal competition-related word primes, wherein competitively predisposed participants played more competitively towards a partner, but only once the partner had made a move that could be interpreted, suggesting that the prime biased how participants construed their partner's behaviour rather than altering their behaviour directly.

text.text: Together, these studies show that primed social concepts can bias the reading of ambiguous interpersonal information.

Whether trustworthiness is open to this same kind of priming first requires distinguishing it from interpersonal trust, which most of the existing priming literature has targeted (Todorov et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Whether trustworthiness is open to this same kind of priming first requires distinguishing it from interpersonal trust, which most of the existing priming literature has targeted <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Todorov et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Interpersonal trust is the willingness to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations about another person's intentions (Mayer et al., 1995; Rousseau et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Interpersonal trust is the willingness to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations about another person's intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Mayer et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Rousseau et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: It is commonly measured with economic trust games, in which a participant entrusts a sum of money to another person; the sum is multiplied, the recipient returns however much they choose, and the amount initially entrusted serves as the behavioural index of trust (Berg et al., 1995; Johnson & Mislin, 2011).
text.formatted: It is commonly measured with economic trust games, in which a participant entrusts a sum of money to another person; the sum is multiplied, the recipient returns however much they choose, and the amount initially entrusted serves as the behavioural index of trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Berg et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Johnson & Mislin, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Trustworthiness, by contrast, is the property attributed to a person that gives rise to that willingness (Mayer et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Trustworthiness, by contrast, is the property attributed to a person that gives rise to that willingness <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Mayer et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The present study targets this latter attribution rather than the behavioural decisions related to trust, so the following evidence is considered with this distinction in mind. Posten et al. (2014) provide a particularly direct test of whether trustworthiness itself can be primed.
text.formatted: The present study targets this latter attribution rather than the behavioural decisions related to trust, so the following evidence is considered with this distinction in mind. <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Posten et al. (2014)</ref> provide a particularly direct test of whether trustworthiness itself can be primed.

text.text: Using a subliminal priming manipulation, they exposed participants to the words trust or distrust and found that unfamiliar faces were subsequently judged more trustworthy following the trust prime than the distrust prime.

The same primes also increased the amount participants sent in a subsequent economic trust game, indicating that the effect extended beyond perceived trustworthiness to trusting behaviour. Verosky and Todorov (2010) similarly showed that minimal behavioural information can alter trustworthiness judgements: after participants learned to associate unfamiliar faces with a single positive, neutral, or negative statement about the person's behaviour, ratings shifted accordingly, and the effect generalised to novel faces that merely resembled the learned ones.
text.formatted: The same primes also increased the amount participants sent in a subsequent economic trust game, indicating that the effect extended beyond perceived trustworthiness to trusting behaviour. <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Verosky and Todorov (2010)</ref> similarly showed that minimal behavioural information can alter trustworthiness judgements: after participants learned to associate unfamiliar faces with a single positive, neutral, or negative statement about the person's behaviour, ratings shifted accordingly, and the effect generalised to novel faces that merely resembled the learned ones.

text.text: Together, these findings show that trustworthiness judgements can be altered by information external to the face itself.
However, both demonstrations rely on relatively direct routes, either providing explicit evaluative information about the person or transferring affect to the face.
It therefore remains unclear whether a more indirect prime, whose social meaning derives from an everyday environment, can produce a similar shift in trustworthiness.
The study that comes closest to addressing this possibility is Huang and Murnighan (2010).
text.formatted: The study that comes closest to addressing this possibility is <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Huang and Murnighan (2010)</ref>.

text.text: Across two experiments, participants first rated the names of people and, in the second experiment, objects as either liked or disliked.
One such name or object was then presented subliminally before participants acted as the sender in an economic trust game.
Participants primed with a liked name sent more money than those primed with either the disliked name or the control name (nonsense syllable).
In contrast, liked and disliked object primes produced no significant difference in the amount sent to the target.

Because the name and object primes were matched in valence using each participant's liked/disliked ratings, the authors argued that the effect depended on the primes' relation to the person rather than on the general pleasantness of the objects or their broader social associations.

They speculated that certain objects may carry particular social connotations that could introduce uncontrolled effects and called for future research to use coherent, socially meaningful object categories to determine whether objectbased primes could influence trust.
Taken together, the literature reviewed above shows that trustworthiness can be shifted by external information.
Still, it leaves unclear whether an everyday object category can do so through its broader social meaning, rather than the idiosyncratic preferences tested previously.
This represents the specific research gap addressed by the present study and has both practical and theoretical significance.
If incidental object cues can bias trustworthiness judgements when information about a person is sparse, they may represent a subtle source of context-dependent bias in social perception.

Such a finding would also provide behavioural evidence that objectderived meaning, like verbal meaning, can influence social perception, potentially through the shared multimodal semantic system outlined earlier.

The present study tests this possibility by comparing three prime categories: home-and workrelated objects, with their contrasting trust-relevant associations, and novel objects with no preexisting trust-relevant meaning.

The Novel category provides a baseline that controls for object exposure and processing, while allowing differences in the Home and Work conditions to be attributed more specifically to social-category content.
Having established trustworthiness as the target judgement, the next choice concerns how to operationalise it: first the form in which it is elicited, and then the instrument used to record it.
The present study elicits trustworthiness judgements from unfamiliar faces.
Such impressions form rapidly and are highly consensual across perceivers (Willis & Todorov, 2006), making them a quick and reliable target.
text.formatted: Such impressions form rapidly and are highly consensual across perceivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Willis & Todorov, 2006)</ref>, making them a quick and reliable target.

text.text: Despite this stability, they remain open to information beyond the face itself.

As noted above, subliminal trust primes and single items of behavioural information can both shift them (Posten et al., 2014; Verosky & Todorov, 2010), and the surrounding social context matters too: for example, faces presented in threatening contexts are rated less trustworthy than the same faces in neutral ones (Brambilla et al., 2018; see also Hooker et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2020; Todorov et al., 2015).
text.formatted: As noted above, subliminal trust primes and single items of behavioural information can both shift them <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Posten et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Verosky & Todorov, 2010)</ref>, and the surrounding social context matters too: for example, faces presented in threatening contexts are rated less trustworthy than the same faces in neutral ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brambilla et al., 2018</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hooker et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cai et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Todorov et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This combination of a fast, consensual judgement that is nonetheless sensitive to context makes facial trustworthiness a suitable outcome for testing whether object primes influence social perception.
Trustworthiness has more often been measured in other ways.

As mentioned, economic trust games (Berg et al., 1995) index the behavioural decision to trust, while dispositional scales such as Rotter's (1967) 25-item Interpersonal Trust Scale measure generalised expectations of others' reliability.

text.text: These capture behavioural trust or a stable disposition rather than the targetspecific impression of interest here (Evans & Revelle, 2008).

(2023)</ref>, which preserves sensitivity to the small, bidirectional shifts the priming manipulation is expected to produce <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Reips & Funke, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: A single-item rating keeps each judgement brief and unobtrusive, and this format yields ratings comparable to those from longer instruments (Bowling, 2005).

text.text: A remaining design choice concerns the onset interval between the prime and target, or stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA).
As set out above, a cross-domain inference from an object to a social category is expected to rely on controlled rather than automatic processing.

Automatic spreading activation is most readily captured at short SOAs of around 250 ms or less (Neely, 1977b; Neely et al., 2010), whereas controlled processing requires a longer interval, typically 400 ms or more, for attention to be redirected (Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2005; Posner & Snyder, 1975).
text.formatted: Automatic spreading activation is most readily captured at short SOAs of around 250 ms or less <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Neely, 1977b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Neely et al., 2010)</ref>, whereas controlled processing requires a longer interval, typically 400 ms or more, for attention to be redirected <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Posner & Snyder, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: The present design therefore uses a 1,000-ms SOA to favour controlled, sustained accessibility over automatic activation (Bargh et al., 1988).

text.text: Conscious presentation nevertheless introduces a potential demand characteristic: participants may notice the manipulation (the change in object categories) and infer the experiment's purpose, a replicability issue that was proposed to have contributed to the inflated weapon-priming effect discussed earlier (Page & Scheidt, 1971; Turner & Simons, 1974).

text.text: The procedure was therefore designed to minimise this possibility (see Procedure).

Finally, because the situated inference model predicts stronger priming when the primed category is more accessible and consistent with the perceiver's dispositions (consistent with the disposition dependence reported by Kay et al., 2004; Neuberg, 1988), exploratory analyses examined whether participants' affective relationships with home and workplace environments and their degree of workplace experience moderated the effects.

text.text: Affective relationships indexed disposition towards each category, whereas workplace experience indexed the availability of work-related representations.
These analyses were underpowered given the present sample size and were not part of the primary test of object-based priming.
Two directional predictions follow.

First, if domestically affiliated objects activate trustrelevant concepts through their association with the home (Collins & Loftus, 1975; Dant, 1999), trustworthiness ratings following Home-object primes will be higher than those following Novel-object primes (H 1 ).

text.text: Second, if Work-affiliated objects activate competition-and self-interest-related concepts, as suggested by Kay et al. (2004), trustworthiness ratings following Work-object primes will be lower than those following Novel-object primes (H 2 ).

text.text: Exploratory analyses will also examine whether individual differences in participants' affective relationships with the home and work environments, and if their workplace experience, moderate these effects.
Thirty participants were recruited using opportunity sampling from the University of St Andrews community.
The recruited sample (24 from Scotland, 3 from England, 2 from the USA, and 1 from Italy; 26 female, 4 male) had a mean age of 24.8 years (SD = 4.9, range 19 to 42).

Inclusion criteria were age ≥ 16 years, fluency in English, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and having been raised in a Western country between the ages of 7 and 15, to ensure shared cultural associations with the object categories (Soley, 2019).
text.formatted: Inclusion criteria were age ≥ 16 years, fluency in English, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and having been raised in a Western country between the ages of 7 and 15, to ensure shared cultural associations with the object categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Soley, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These criteria were stated prior to booking and confirmed on arrival via a yes/no screening questionnaire covering childhood upbringing, vision, age, fluency, and willingness to participate; answering "no" to any item prevented continuation.

Two participants were subsequently excluded during data screening, leaving a final analysed sample of N = 28 (see Data Handling and Exclusions); because data were anonymised at collection, the demographic characteristics reported here describe the full recruited sample.
The subsections below describe the a priori power analysis, recruitment procedure, exclusion criteria, and ethical considerations.

A simulation-based a priori power analysis was conducted using the simr package (Version 1.0.9; Green & MacLeod, 2016) in R (Version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026), following recommendations for linear mixed models (LMM; Kumle et al., 2021; Meteyard & Davies, 2020).

text.text: A dataset was simulated to reflect a one-way within-subjects design with three condition categories (Home, Work, Novel), each providing 10 trials per condition (840 total observations) for a presumed sample of 28 participants.

The final design included 15 trials per condition; the lower simulated trial count of 10 therefore provided a conservative estimate that accounted for potential trial losses, as participants could skip trials during the experiment.
A small-to-medium effect size was specified (β = 3; f = 0.15), below Kay et al.'s (2004) reported effects (partial η² = 0.13 to 0.32; f = 0.39 to 0.69).

text.text: Based on 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations of the specified model parameters (seed = 2025 for reproducibility, powerSim, α = 0.05), the analysis returned 81.90% power (95% CI [79.37, 84.24]) at 28 participants.
The power curve indicated that 80% was reached between 25 and 28 participants.
Therefore, a recruitment target of 30 participants was set to increase power further and allow for potential participant exclusions.
Participants were recruited using opportunity sampling via university email circulars, online noticeboards, and printed posters distributed across the University of St Andrews campus.

All recruitment materials were deliberately general and did not disclose the study aims (e.g., the role of the object stimuli or the hypothesised direction of effects), to minimise demand characteristics (Nichols & Maner, 2008) and preserve the integrity of the manipulation (Doyen et al., 2012).
text.formatted: All recruitment materials were deliberately general and did not disclose the study aims (e.g., the role of the object stimuli or the hypothesised direction of effects), to minimise demand characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Nichols & Maner, 2008)</ref> and preserve the integrity of the manipulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Doyen et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals who registered interest were shown the participant information sheet (PIS) to verify eligibility and, if eligible, were invited to book an in-person session.
Participation was entirely voluntary, and no individuals were approached directly.
Recruitment took place between May and July 2026.

Exclusion criteria were specified as follows and participant data were excluded if any of the criteria applied: (a) failure of the comprehension-check following the task instructions; (b) total task completion time falling more than 50% below or above the sample mean, indicating either rushed non-engagement or interrupted responding, following duration-based screening practice for computer-administered tasks (Meade & Craig, 2012); (c) identical responses on ≥ 50% of consecutive trustworthiness ratings, indicating straight-lining (see Maniaci & Rogge, 2014; Meade & Craig, 2012); (d) failure on two or more of the three embedded attention-check items; or (e) a non-response rate exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials, which would reduce the percondition trial count below the 10-trial minimum specified in the a priori power analysis (see above).

text.text: The study was assessed as minimal risk and approved by the University of St Andrews Teaching and Research Ethics Committee (UTREC; approval reference PS-1485-2292-2026).

Full hypothesis disclosure was withheld at the outset to prevent demand characteristics; this incomplete disclosure was judged proportionate to the minimal risk of the study and mitigated by disclosure within the debrief.
Potential discomfort from home or workplace content was addressed through a generalised PIS, freedom to withdraw without penalty, and signposting to student support services at debrief.
Compensation was fixed at £10, non-contingent on performance or completion, consistent with University guidance and the current UK National Living Wage (effective April 1 st 2026; GOV.UK, 2026).
Sessions lasted ~30 minutes.
Data collection took place between May and July 2026.
Data were anonymised at collection and stored on the University's encrypted OneDrive system.

The researcher did not collect payment details; they were handled by the School Finance Administrator, stored in the University's encrypted OneDrive system, separate from the research data, and deleted once payment processing was complete.
The task was administered via the Gorilla experiment platform, accessed through a web browser running on macOS 26.6.1.
The experimental interface and stimuli were displayed on an external 24-inch (16:9) LCD monitor (1920 × 1080 pixels, 60 Hz) at a viewing distance of ~80 cm, maintained with a forehead-and-chin rest.
Responses were recorded via a standard QWERTY keyboard and mouse.

Object images were drawn from the IMAGINE database (Cooper et al., 2023), which provides standardised photographs of familiar objects and computer-generated images of "Novel objects" presented in a common photographic style against a uniform white background.
text.formatted: Object images were drawn from the IMAGINE database <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Cooper et al., 2023)</ref>, which provides standardised photographs of familiar objects and computer-generated images of "Novel objects" presented in a common photographic style against a uniform white background.

text.text: Images were normalised for low-level visual attributes including size, contrast, colourfulness, luminance and resolution.
From the familiar object set, 48 images were selected and recategorised into two sub-categories of 24 images each: home objects (the experimental primes) and work objects (the contrast primes).
A further 24 images were drawn at random from the novel objects set to serve as control primes, yielding 72 total prime stimuli across three categories, each of equal size (Figure 1).
text.formatted: A further 24 images were drawn at random from the novel objects set to serve as control primes, yielding 72 total prime stimuli across three categories, each of equal size (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

(2023) IMAGINE database.
The full stimulus set comprised 24 images per category (Home, Work, Novel) for a total of 72 priming stimuli.
All images are normalised for size, contrast, luminance, and colourfulness and presented against a uniform white background.
Home objects (experimental primes): Items strongly associated with domestic spaces (e.g., an ironing board and teapot).

The selection of canonical household items was guided by the material-culture literature as identified above (Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981; Dant, 1999), and for their broad recognisability across Western domestic contexts.

text.text: Work objects (contrast primes): Items strongly associated with workplace environments (e.g., manila files, filing cabinet, executive pen).
The category was guided by the material-culture literature (Fiske, 1991; Hodder, 2012; Nippert-Eng, 1996) and defined in accordance with Kay et al. (2004).

(2004)</ref>.

text.text: Novel objects (control primes): AI-generated images that present as objects but lack identifiable real-world referents, randomly drawn from the Novel-object subset of Cooper et al. (2023).
text.formatted: Novel objects (control primes): AI-generated images that present as objects but lack identifiable real-world referents, randomly drawn from the Novel-object subset of <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Cooper et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: These provide a baseline that indexes responses to a visual stimulus in the absence of meaningful contextual or semantic associations.

Face stimuli were drawn from the Oosterhof and Todorov (2008) database, consisting of computer-generated faces varying parametrically along trustworthiness and dominance dimensions, generated in FaceGen Modeller 3.2.
text.formatted: Face stimuli were drawn from the <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Oosterhof and Todorov (2008)</ref> database, consisting of computer-generated faces varying parametrically along trustworthiness and dominance dimensions, generated in FaceGen Modeller 3.2.

text.text: All faces were male, bald, Caucasian and front-facing, with neutral expressions and a direct gaze (Figure 2).
text.formatted: All faces were male, bald, Caucasian and front-facing, with neutral expressions and a direct gaze (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: To isolate trustworthiness, dominance was held constant at its midpoint (dominance = 0).
The trustworthiness dimension was sampled at seven equally spaced levels, from very untrustworthy (-3) to very trustworthy (+3).
The samples were gathered through the "490 Faces (2 orthogonal models)" database by extracting items 3, 10, 17, 24, 31, 38 and 45 from each identity file 1 to 10.
Example face stimuli from the Oosterhof and Todorov (2008) database Untrustworthy (trust value = -3) Trustworthy (trust value = +3) Note.
