text.text: Both faces were generated from the same underlying identity (identity 1) and show the two extremes of the sampled trustworthiness range.
The trustworthiness dimension was sampled at seven equally spaced levels (-3, -2, -1, 0, +1, +2, +3), with dominance held constant at zero (Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008).
text.formatted: The trustworthiness dimension was sampled at seven equally spaced levels (-3, -2, -1, 0, +1, +2, +3), with dominance held constant at zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Of the 10 identities available, identities 1 to 9 supplied the main trustworthiness trials, retaining five of the seven levels (-3, -1, 0, +1, +3), yielding 45 usable face stimuli.

The omitted levels (-2 and +2) across identities 1 to 9, together with all seven levels of identity 10, were reserved (and when necessary, presented more than once) for the catch, filler and attention-check trials described in the Procedure, ensuring that faces contributing to the analysis were not those used to obscure the hypothesis or verify engagement.
Trustworthiness was rated using a single-item visual analogue scale (VAS), adapted from Pehlivanoglu et al. (2023).
text.formatted: Trustworthiness was rated using a single-item visual analogue scale (VAS), adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Pehlivanoglu et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: For analysed trials, each participant was asked, "How trustworthy is this face?"
and responded by moving a slider along a continuous horizontal line, anchored at 0 ("Not at all trustworthy") to 100 ("Extremely trustworthy").

This continuous format was selected to avoid the response compression inherent to discrete Likert scales (Reips & Funke, 2008) and to allow participants to directly map their immediate, pre-reflective gut response onto a spatial continuum -bypassing the discrete categorisation that would disrupt the rapid first impressions of trustworthiness targeted by the manipulation (Bowling, 2005; Castle et al., 2012; Evans & Revelle, 2008; Willis & Todorov, 2006).
text.formatted: This continuous format was selected to avoid the response compression inherent to discrete Likert scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Reips & Funke, 2008)</ref> and to allow participants to directly map their immediate, pre-reflective gut response onto a spatial continuum -bypassing the discrete categorisation that would disrupt the rapid first impressions of trustworthiness targeted by the manipulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bowling, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Castle et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Evans & Revelle, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Willis & Todorov, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Three self-reported items were administered at the end of the session, after debriefing, to index participants' evaluation of home environments, their evaluation of workplace environments, and their degree of workplace exposure, for use in the exploratory analyses.
Each exploratory item appeared on separate sliders and used a continuous 0 to 100 VAS, consistent with the VAS measures used in the experimental phase (Bowling, 2005).
text.formatted: Each exploratory item appeared on separate sliders and used a continuous 0 to 100 VAS, consistent with the VAS measures used in the experimental phase <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bowling, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Administering these items after the debriefing prevented participants from recognising the Home/Work prime categories; however, it also means that the affiliation ratings index a state measured after exposure to the primes, which may affect their accuracy (Howard et al., 1979).
text.formatted: Administering these items after the debriefing prevented participants from recognising the Home/Work prime categories; however, it also means that the affiliation ratings index a state measured after exposure to the primes, which may affect their accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Howard et al., 1979)</ref>.

text.text: The three items were: (i) "How positive is your overall relationship with the home environments you have lived in?", anchored at0 = "extremely negative" and100 = "extremely positive"; (ii) "How positive is your overall relationship with the workplace or office environments you have experienced?", anchored at0 = "extremely negative" and100 = "extremely positive"; (iii) "How much personal experience do you have with traditional workplace or office environments (for example, paid work in an office)?", anchored at0 = "no experience at all" and100 = "a great deal of experience".
Sessions were run individually, under the supervision of the experimenter, in the University of St Andrews School of Psychology and Neuroscience 3D Vision lab.
The forehead-and-chin rest used in the study held viewing distance and visual angle constant across participants and restricted the participant's field of view to the screen.

The latter precaution was important as the laboratory itself contains some workplace-affiliated objects (e.g., filing cabinets, office furniture) potentially capable of raising work-related associations independent of the experimental primes (Kay et al., 2004).
text.formatted: The latter precaution was important as the laboratory itself contains some workplace-affiliated objects (e.g., filing cabinets, office furniture) potentially capable of raising work-related associations independent of the experimental primes <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Kay et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Ambient lighting was held consistent across sessions and external noise was minimised.
The study employed a within-subjects priming design with the three prime categories (Home, Work, and Novel).
Participants rated face trustworthiness (0 to 100 VAS) across 45 trials split evenly across prime categories, yielding repeated measures at both participant and item (face) levels.

Each participant completed one of three Gorilla spreadsheets (i.e., trial structures), which intermixed the trust, filler, and catch trials, while the three attention checks were held at fixed positions across all versions to maintain an even spread throughout the experiment.
Within each spreadsheet, prime frequencies and face-trustworthiness levels were balanced every ~10 trials (across 7 blocks), to prevent consistent prime-face pairings.
The design also included the three (post-debrief) affiliation probe items, which assessed participants' individual category preferences.

This follows established priming paradigms (Bargh et al., 1996; Kay et al., 2004) while adhering to replicability recommendations regarding power and counterbalancing (Doyen et al., 2012; Munafò et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This follows established priming paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bargh et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kay et al., 2004)</ref> while adhering to replicability recommendations regarding power and counterbalancing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Doyen et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Munafò et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: On arrival, participants viewed the PIS on screen and ticked confirmation boxes to confirm they had read each section, met eligibility, and provided consent; Gorilla prevented progression to the experimental phase unless all boxes were ticked.

Participants then completed a brief tutorial (one demonstrated trial and three practice trials, all using the 0 to 100 VAS) involving fillerstyle perceptual judgements (e.g., age) of faces and displayed random images from the Cooper et al. (2023) database, unrelated to the experimental prime categories.
text.formatted: Participants then completed a brief tutorial (one demonstrated trial and three practice trials, all using the 0 to 100 VAS) involving fillerstyle perceptual judgements (e.g., age) of faces and displayed random images from the <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Cooper et al. (2023)</ref> database, unrelated to the experimental prime categories.

text.text: This familiarised participants with the interface without directing attention to trust or the Home/Work/Novel categories.

Following the tutorial, participants completed a short comprehension check confirming that they understood the task instructions and the use of the slider; failure to answer all items correctly met exclusion criterion (a).

This was then followed by the experimental phase, which comprised 73 trials in total: 45 main trustworthiness trials, 18 filler trials, 7 catch trials, and 3 attention checks, distributed across the 7 blocks, with three self-paced breaks.

The 45 main trustworthiness trials each proceeded as follows: central fixation cross (2,000 ms), object prime (1,000 ms), second fixation cross (1,000 ms), face stimulus (1,000 ms), self-paced trustworthiness rating (0 to 100 VAS; "How trustworthy is this face?"), and a 2,000 ms inter-trial interval.

Filler trials (×18) were scattered throughout to interrupt the sequence of trustworthiness questions and reduce participants' ability to infer the hypothesis; these used the main trial structure but asked about a different facial attribute on the same 0 to 100 VAS (age, dominance, approachability, attractiveness, intelligence, or health; e.g., "How healthy does this face look?").
Catch trials (×7) required a response about the object prime rather than the face, to sustain participants' attention to the primes (e.g., "How clearly do you remember the object you just saw?"
from 0 "not at all" to 100 "extremely well").

Attention checks (×3) were fixed at trials 16, 38, and 57 across the three spreadsheets; these presented explicit instructions (e.g., "Please move the slider all the way to one hundred, to show you are reading") to comply with exclusion criterion (d).
Three self-paced breaks were positioned at trials 22, 44, and 66, each carrying the message: "Take a break; take as long as you need and press continue when ready".
Participants then received a written debrief describing the study's rationale, which also provided the researcher's contact details.
After the debrief, they completed the two Home/Work affiliation items alongside the work experience item (described above).

Two participants were excluded for non-response exceeding 30% of trustworthiness trials (31.1% and 64.4% missing respectively) as per exclusion criteria (e); no other exclusion criteria (a-d) were met, leaving a final analytic sample of N = 28 and 1,217 valid trustworthiness-rating trials (Novel n = 410, Home n = 403, and Work n = 404) across all participants.
Anonymisation prevented participant characteristic linkage post-exclusion.
Among the retained participants only 3.4% of trials were missing (43 of 1,260); these did not contribute to the model, which was fitted to all trials with complete data.

Missingness was unrelated to prime condition and related only to face-trust level, a variable already in the model (see Appendix B), so the data can plausibly be treated as missing at random, under which restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation (the method used to fit the models below), remains unbiased.
Filler and catch trials were excluded prior to model fitting.
The analysis is a within-participant comparison: it asks whether trustworthiness ratings differ across the three prime conditions (Home, Work, Novel).

What complicates a simple comparison is the repeated-measures design, as each participant rated every face identity and level, so trials were correlated both within participants and within face identities (Baayen et al., 2008); a linear regression would treat all 1,217 trials as independent and understate the standard errors (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: What complicates a simple comparison is the repeated-measures design, as each participant rated every face identity and level, so trials were correlated both within participants and within face identities <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baayen et al., 2008)</ref>; a linear regression would treat all 1,217 trials as independent and understate the standard errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) is the appropriate tool here, running the same comparison of prime conditions while allowing each participant and each face their own baseline rating, so that repeated ratings from the same person or face are not mistaken for effects of the primes (Baayen et al., 2008; see also Brown, 2021).
text.formatted: Therefore, a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) is the appropriate tool here, running the same comparison of prime conditions while allowing each participant and each face their own baseline rating, so that repeated ratings from the same person or face are not mistaken for effects of the primes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baayen et al., 2008</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Brown, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, crossed random intercepts were specified for participant and face identity (28 participants, 9 face identities), modelling both sources directly (Baayen et al., 2008; Judd et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Consequently, crossed random intercepts were specified for participant and face identity (28 participants, 9 face identities), modelling both sources directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baayen et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Judd et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The model was estimated by REML, which is the recommended estimation method when interpreting random effects in a single fitted model (Bates et al., 2015), with Satterthwaite (1946) approximate degrees of freedom used to evaluate fixed effects given that exact degrees of freedom cannot be determined analytically in mixed models.
text.formatted: The model was estimated by REML, which is the recommended estimation method when interpreting random effects in a single fitted model <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Satterthwaite (1946)</ref> approximate degrees of freedom used to evaluate fixed effects given that exact degrees of freedom cannot be determined analytically in mixed models.

text.text: Statistical significance was evaluated at α = .05.
All statistical analyses were conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics (Version 31; macOS).
All figures were produced in R (Version 4.6.1, using the ggplot2, ggeffects, lme4 and haven packages; macOS).

Model assumptions were assessed; a full list of the assumptions and the procedures used are reported in Appendix A. Face identity was treated as a random effect throughout, its intercept retained because the repeated-measures design requires it.
Random slopes for prime were not fitted; the rationale, and the safeguard applied to any significant prime effect, are described in Appendix A.
A trial-level LMM was fitted to the trustworthiness ratings, estimated on 1,217 valid trials from the final analytic sample (N = 28).

This main-effects model (Model 1) included two dummycoded prime variables (prime_home and prime_work) and a continuous covariate for the normative trustworthiness level of each face (face_trust_level) based on Oosterhof and Todorov's (2008) original rankings.
text.formatted: This main-effects model (Model 1) included two dummycoded prime variables (prime_home and prime_work) and a continuous covariate for the normative trustworthiness level of each face (face_trust_level) based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Oosterhof and Todorov's (2008)</ref> original rankings.

text.text: A significant prime term would indicate that the preceding object category (Home and/or Work) shifted how trustworthy the face appeared relative to the Novel baseline and each face's own normative trustworthiness, which the covariate holds constant.
Two further models were then fitted.

Model 2 added prime × face-trust level interaction terms, testing whether any priming effect varied across the trustworthiness dimension (i.e., whether the primes mattered more for some faces than others).
Model 3 replaced these with prime × ambiguity interactions, comparing ambiguous faces (normative levels -1 to +1) with unambiguous faces (±3).

A significant prime × ambiguity interaction would indicate that the prime effect differed by the face's ambiguity, consistent with the expectation that primes exert more influence when the target is ambiguous.
Together, these two models tested whether any prime effects were concentrated among particular faces rather than spread evenly across the trustworthiness dimension.

The two prime contrasts (Home, Work) and face-trust level all vary within participants and within face identities and are therefore trial-level (level-1) predictors; the model includes no predictor that varies between participants or between faces (i.e., no level-2 predictor); whether effects differed between participants is taken up separately in the following exploratory analyses.
The model is specified in full in Appendix A.
The first exploratory analysis asks whether the primes worked differently for different people.
It was motivated a priori by the situated inference model (Loersch & Payne, 2011), which holds that a prime exerts a stronger influence when the primed category fits the perceiver's own dispositions.
text.formatted: It was motivated a priori by the situated inference model <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>, which holds that a prime exerts a stronger influence when the primed category fits the perceiver's own dispositions.

text.text: If so, participants who feel more positively about home than work environments, or the reverse, might respond differently to Home and Work primes, an effect that could be masked in the sample as a whole.

Participants were grouped by their differences in Home and Work affiliation ratings, classifying participants as Home-leaning (Home > Work by more than 20 points), Work-leaning (Work > Home by more than 20 points), or Balanced (all remaining participants).
text.formatted: Participants were grouped by their differences in Home and Work affiliation ratings, classifying participants as Home-leaning (Home > Work by more than 20 points), Work-leaning (Work > Home by more than 20 points), or Balanced (all remaining participants).

text.text: Group membership was dummy-coded with Balanced as the reference category, yielding two dummy variables (Home-leaning vs Balanced; Work-leaning vs Balanced); these were entered into the trial-level model alongside all four resulting Prime Category × Group interactions.

The random structure and estimation method were as described above, the mixed-effects framework being retained as the same two crossed sources of non-independence apply and because it estimates the group contrasts at the participant level while retaining all trials.
The assumption checks described for the primary analysis (Appendix A) were repeated for this model, because residuals are model-specific (Brown, 2021; Field, 2024; Meteyard & Davies, 2020).
text.formatted: The assumption checks described for the primary analysis (Appendix A) were repeated for this model, because residuals are model-specific <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Brown, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Field, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Meteyard & Davies, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Two features of this analysis limit how far its results can be interpreted.
First, four Prime Category × Group interactions are tested simultaneously, so the probability that at least one reaches p < .05 by chance alone is ~19% rather than 5%.
text.formatted: First, four Prime Category × Group interactions are tested simultaneously, so the probability that at least one reaches p < .05 by chance alone is ~19% rather than 5%.

text.text: The significance threshold for this family of tests was therefore Bonferroni-corrected to α = .0125 (.05 / 4; Field, 2024).

Therefore, any interaction reaching the conventional threshold (α = .05) but not the corrected threshold, was treated as tentative at most and followed up with a focused sensitivity analysis, in which that term was tested in isolation against all other participants to assess its robustness to the grouping specification.
Second, and more fundamentally, affiliation group is a characteristic of the participant, not of the trial.
Its interactions with the primes are therefore estimated between participants (a level-2 comparison across only 28 individuals) rather than across the 1,217 trials.
These estimates draw their power from the number of participants per group, not the trial count, which makes them far less precise than the primary effects.
The results of this analysis are accordingly treated as exploratory and should be interpreted with caution (Field, 2024).
text.formatted: The results of this analysis are accordingly treated as exploratory and should be interpreted with caution <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Field, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The final analysis follows the same accessibility logic as the profile group analysis.
Applied to the full analytic sample, it tested whether individual differences in workplace exposure moderated priming effects.

Planned a priori from theory, it was motivated by the situated inference model (Loersch & Payne, 2011), which holds that a prime influences judgement only when the primed representation is accessible, so participants with greater workplace exposure, and thus more accessible work-related representations, should show a stronger Work prime effect.
text.formatted: Planned a priori from theory, it was motivated by the situated inference model <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>, which holds that a prime influences judgement only when the primed representation is accessible, so participants with greater workplace exposure, and thus more accessible work-related representations, should show a stronger Work prime effect.

text.text: The prediction therefore concerns the Work prime specifically: a significant Work prime × experience interaction would indicate that the Work prime shifted trustworthiness ratings more strongly in participants with more workplace exposure.
The Home prime interaction was included for symmetry but has no corresponding theoretical basis.
Self-reported work experience (range 0 to 100, M = 40.36, SD = 36.68) was mean-centred and entered as a fixed effect together with its interactions with each prime contrast.

All other modelling choices, including the crossed random-intercept structure, estimation method and assumption checks, were as described for the primary analysis; because residuals are model-specific, they were reapplied to this model (see Appendix A).
As with the profile groups, work experience is a between-participant (level-2) predictor and its prime interactions are therefore, cross-level interactions estimated across only 28 participants.
This is the lower bound for such tests, leaving the moderation underpowered by construction (Hox et al., 2018); its results should therefore be read with caution and as hypothesis-generating only.
text.formatted: This is the lower bound for such tests, leaving the moderation underpowered by construction <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hox et al., 2018)</ref>; its results should therefore be read with caution and as hypothesis-generating only.

text.text: A linear mixed-effects model with crossed random intercepts for participant and face identity was fitted to the 1,217 valid trials, as specified above.
Model diagnostics and variance components supported the adequacy of this random-effects structure (see Appendix B).
Figure 3 shows the observed pattern of the data.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref> shows the observed pattern of the data.

text.text: Ratings increased steadily with the normative face-trust level, while the three prime conditions closely overlapped across the range.
Thus, participants tracked the intended differences in facial trustworthiness, but the preceding object primes produced little visible change in ratings.

Mean trustworthiness ratings (0 to 100 VAS) by normative face-trust level (-3 to +3; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008) for Novel n = 410, Home n = 403, and Work n = 404 primes (N = 28; 1,217 total trials).
text.formatted: Mean trustworthiness ratings (0 to 100 VAS) by normative face-trust level (-3 to +3; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008) for Novel n = 410, Home n = 403, and Work n = 404 primes (N = 28; 1,217 total trials).

text.text: Error bars show descriptive 95% CIs from observed cell data; unlike Table 2, they do not account for crossed participant and face-identity random effects.
The common upward pattern reflects the face-trust effect, whereas the three overlapping prime lines indicate no reliable main effect or prime × face-trust interaction.
The model was consistent with this descriptive pattern.

Normative face trustworthiness strongly predicted participants' ratings: each one-unit increase in the face's normative trust level was associated with a 4.61-point increase in ratings across the 0 to 100 scale (b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001), confirming that participants tracked the intended trustworthiness dimension (Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008).
text.formatted: Normative face trustworthiness strongly predicted participants' ratings: each one-unit increase in the face's normative trust level was associated with a 4.61-point increase in ratings across the 0 to 100 scale (b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001), confirming that participants tracked the intended trustworthiness dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, neither object-prime effect reached conventional significance: relative to Novel objects, Home primes were associated with a 2.23point increase in ratings (b = 2.23, 95% CI [-0.10, 4.56], p = .061), while Work primes were associated with a similar 2.08-point increase (b = 2.08, 95% CI [-0.21, 4.38], p = .075).
Both effects were therefore small and in the same direction, corresponding to modest increases in trustworthiness ratings.

The Home effect was thus consistent with the predicted direction, whereas the Work effect was opposite to the predicted reduction, with the two priming effects statistically indistinguishable from each other, b = 0.13, 95% CI [-2.18, 2.43], p = .913 (Figure 4).
text.formatted: The Home effect was thus consistent with the predicted direction, whereas the Work effect was opposite to the predicted reduction, with the two priming effects statistically indistinguishable from each other, b = 0.13, 95% CI [-2.18, 2.43], p = .913 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>).

text.text: Both confidence intervals included zero, so the data are compatible with no effect of either prime (Appendix B, Table 2).

Points are the estimated differences in trustworthiness rating (0 to 100 VAS) between each prime condition and the Novel baseline, from the primary trial-level mixed-effects model; error bars are 95% confidence intervals.
The dashed line marks no difference from the Novel baseline.
A second model assessed whether the primes mattered more for some faces than others by adding prime × face-trust level (FTL) interaction terms.

They did not: the small prime effects were relatively constant across face-trust levels (Home × FTL, b = 0.41, 95% CI [-0.75, 1.56], p = .488; Work × FTL, b = 0.24, 95% CI [-0.92, 1.41], p = .685; Figure 3).

text.text: A further model tested whether priming effects differed between ambiguous (-1 to +1) and unambiguous (±3) faces, given the greater potential susceptibility of ambiguous faces to priming (Higgins et al., 1977; Kay et al., 2004).

text.text: Neither interaction was significant (Home × ambiguity, b = 2.18, 95% CI [-3.25, 7.60], p = .431; Work × ambiguity, b = 1.32, 95% CI [-4.19, 6.82], p = .638), and the ambiguity main effect was also non-significant (b = 1.20, 95% CI [-2.62, 5.01], p = .538).
There was therefore no evidence that the effects of the primes varied according to face-trust level or face ambiguity.
One trial had a large standardised residual (3.40, exceeding the conventional |z| > 3.29 threshold; see Appendix B).
text.formatted: One trial had a large standardised residual (3.40, exceeding the conventional |z| > 3.29 threshold; see Appendix B).

text.text: Since this outlier was a Novel prime condition, removing it could shift the Novel baseline that both prime contrasts are measured against, so it was retained in the primary model and its influence checked by re-fitting the model without it.

When refitted, the direction of all effects was unchanged, however, the Home-versus-Novel contrast now reached conventional significance (b = 2.40, 95% CI [0.08, 4.72], p = .043), while the Work-versus-Novel contrast remained just short of significance (p = .053).
Therefore, the evidence for a priming effect was somewhat sensitive to this single trial.

However, because both primeversus-Novel contrasts increased when the trial was removed, the change appears to reflect, at least in part, a change in the estimated Novel reference level rather than a uniquely increased Home effect.
Full estimates are reported in Appendix B.

The first exploratory analysis tested whether participants' relative affiliation with Home versus Work moderated the effects of the object primes on trustworthiness ratings, comparing Homeleaning and Work-leaning participants with the Balanced group.
Applying the Home-minus-Work difference rule yielded three groups: Home-leaning (n = 5; ≤225 trials), Work-leaning (n = 4; ≤180 trials), and Balanced (n = 19; ≤855 trials).
The model was fitted to the same 1,217 trials from N = 28 participants and 9 face identities as the primary analysis.
As in the primary model, random intercepts were specified for participants and face identities, and model assumptions were checked and were satisfactory (see Appendix C).
The estimated variance components and ICCs were also similar to those of the primary model (see Appendix C).
Overall, there was little evidence that affiliation systematically altered the prime effects.
Face baseline trustworthiness remained the strongest predictor and was essentially unchanged from the primary model (b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001).
text.formatted: Face baseline trustworthiness remained the strongest predictor and was essentially unchanged from the primary model (b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001).

text.text: Within the Balanced reference group, neither prime reliably shifted ratings (Home, b = 1.26, 95% CI [-1.53, 4.05], p = .375; Work, b = 1.81, 95% CI [-0.97, 4.60], p = .201).

Nonetheless, one interaction reached the conventional threshold (α = .05), but not the Bonferroni-corrected one (α = .0125): the Homeversus-Novel contrast was ~6.6 points larger among Home-leaning than Balanced participants (b = 6.59, 95% CI [0.52, 12.66], p = .033).

However, this interaction is difficult to interpret reliably as a Home-specific priming effect, since Home-leaning participants also tended to rate Novel-primed faces lower than the Balanced group (b = -6.87, 95% CI [-14.00, 0.26], p = .058; Figure 5).

text.text: The interaction's robustness to a by-participant random-slope structure could not be established, as that model did not converge (Appendix C).
The other three prime × group interactions were non-significant (Appendix C, Table 3).

text.text: Additionally, the observed interaction remained similar when the outlier trial was removed (b = 6.39, p = .038; see Appendix C), indicating that the interaction was not substantially altered by that single Novel trial.
Note.
Ratings represent mean trustworthiness judgements on a 0 to 100 visual analogue scale following Novel primes for Home-leaning (n = 5), Work-leaning (n = 4), and Balanced (n = 19) participants.
Error bars represent descriptive 95% confidence intervals based on betweenparticipant variability within each group.

Since dividing participants at a fixed cut-off discards information about how strongly each participant leaned towards Home or Work, the moderation was re-examined with the Homeminus-Work affiliation score entered as a continuous predictor.
This reproduced the same pattern: the Home prime effect increased as participants became more Home-leaning (Home prime × affiliation, b = 0.10, 95% CI [0.002, 0.189], p = .046).
Thus, each one-point increase in Home-leaning affiliation was associated with an ~0.10-point increase in the Home prime effect relative to the Novel condition.
By contrast, the Work prime effect showed no such moderation (p = .181).

However, the Home prime interaction was sensitive to how affiliation was specified and weakened to non-significance when the five Home-leaning participants were instead compared against all other participants combined (i.e., Work-leaning and Balanced; b = 4.93, p = .062).

The exploratory analyses therefore point to a possible stronger Home priming effect among more Home-leaning participants; however, this evidence is tentative as the effect rests on a small subgroup of participants and changes depending on how the comparison group is defined.
Full analyses are reported in Appendix C.

The final analysis tested whether work experience moderated the effects of the object primes, on the reasoning that greater exposure to workplace environments might make work-related associations more accessible and therefore increase sensitivity to the primes (Loersch & Payne, 2011).
text.formatted: The final analysis tested whether work experience moderated the effects of the object primes, on the reasoning that greater exposure to workplace environments might make work-related associations more accessible and therefore increase sensitivity to the primes <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: All assumptions were checked and were satisfactory, and random-intercept specifications were equivalent to those of the primary model; the variance components and model diagnostics differed only slightly and were non-consequential (see Appendix D).
The analysis provided no evidence of moderation.

As in the primary analysis, face baseline trustworthiness strongly predicted ratings, b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001, while the Home-versus-Novel contrast (b = 2.23, p = .061) and the Work-versus-Novel contrast (b = 2.08, p = .075) remained small and non-significant.
text.formatted: As in the primary analysis, face baseline trustworthiness strongly predicted ratings, b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001, while the Home-versus-Novel contrast (b = 2.23, p = .061) and the Work-versus-Novel contrast (b = 2.08, p = .075) remained small and non-significant.

text.text: Thus, the pattern of the primary prime effects was unchanged when work experience was included in the model.

Work experience itself was not associated with overall trustworthiness ratings, b = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.07], p = .796, indicating no evidence that participants with more work experience rated the faces differently overall.

More importantly, neither prime × work experience interaction was significant: the Home prime × work experience interaction was b = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.10], p = .217, and the Work prime × work experience interaction was b = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.09], p = .491.
These results provide no evidence that work experience altered the effect of either object category on trustworthiness ratings.
Furthermore, these conclusions were unchanged when the outlier trial was removed (see Appendix D).
The purpose of this study was to test whether everyday objects carry socially relevant meanings capable of influencing how people judge others.

Specifically, it asked whether an object's membership of a broad social category, the home or the workplace, could shift the trustworthiness attributed to an unfamiliar face, following the call by Huang and Murnighan (2010) for research using coherent, socially meaningful object categories.
text.formatted: Specifically, it asked whether an object's membership of a broad social category, the home or the workplace, could shift the trustworthiness attributed to an unfamiliar face, following the call by <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Huang and Murnighan (2010)</ref> for research using coherent, socially meaningful object categories.

text.text: Two directional hypotheses were set out in a data analysis plan before the data were analysed: trustworthiness ratings following Home-object primes would be higher than those following Novel-object primes (H₁), and ratings following Work-object primes would be lower than those following Novel-object primes (H₂).
Exploratory analyses would then examine whether participants' affective relationships with the home and work environments, and their workplace experience, moderated these effects.
Neither hypothesis was supported.
Home and Work primes instead produced small, similar, non-significant increases relative to Novel objects, so the study did not produce the categoryspecific divergence it was designed to detect.

Because no manipulation check was included, the design cannot separate a failure of the objects to activate their intended constructs from a failure of those constructs to bear on the judgement (see Limitations and Future Directions).

This study examined whether everyday objects carry socially relevant meanings capable of influencing how people judge others, specifically whether brief exposure to home-related, work-related, or novel objects would alter the trustworthiness attributed to unfamiliar faces.

This question has practical significance because incidental environmental cues that influence trustworthiness judgements could represent a subtle and largely unrecognised source of context-dependent bias in everyday social perception.
Participants therefore rated the trustworthiness of unfamiliar faces following brief exposure to an object prime.

The data were examined in three ways: a primary test of whether prime category influenced trustworthiness judgements, an exploratory test of whether participants' affiliation with home or work environments moderated this effect, and a further test of whether workplace experience did so.
Across all three analyses, object primes produced no reliable effect on trustworthiness, and the exploratory affiliation effect was not robust to further sensitivity analysis.
Each analysis and its implications are considered in turn below.
The trial-level LMM provided no clear evidence that prime category influenced trustworthiness ratings.
Neither directional hypothesis was supported: Home primes did not significantly increase ratings (H 1 ), and Work primes did not significantly decrease them (H 2 ).
Instead, both contrasts were positive and similar in magnitude, rather than opposing in direction as predicted (Home, b = 2.23, p = .061; Work, b = 2.08, p = .075).
Although small effects cannot be ruled out entirely, these near-threshold values should be read with caution.
The model omitted a perparticipant random slope for prime (a deliberate simplification; see Appendix A), and omitting such slopes inflates the risk of false positives (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The model omitted a perparticipant random slope for prime (a deliberate simplification; see Appendix A), and omitting such slopes inflates the risk of false positives <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Any prime effect is therefore unlikely to be stronger than the estimates reported here.
There was also no evidence that any prime effect was concentrated among face-types.

Neither prime interacted with normative face-trustworthiness level, nor face ambiguity, where the lack of contextual information was expected to exert greater influence on the judgement (Cesario, 2014; Loersch & Payne, 2011).
text.formatted: Neither prime interacted with normative face-trustworthiness level, nor face ambiguity, where the lack of contextual information was expected to exert greater influence on the judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Cesario, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, normative facial trustworthiness strongly predicted participants' trust ratings (b = 4.61, p < .001), indicating that the measure was sensitive to the judgement being made.
text.formatted: At the same time, normative facial trustworthiness strongly predicted participants' trust ratings (b = 4.61, p < .001), indicating that the measure was sensitive to the judgement being made.

text.text: This, together with evidence that trustworthiness judgements of such faces are susceptible to task-relevant priming (Posten et al., 2014), provides little indication that the null finding resulted from an insensitive measure or a paradigm inherently incapable of priming.
text.formatted: This, together with evidence that trustworthiness judgements of such faces are susceptible to task-relevant priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Posten et al., 2014)</ref>, provides little indication that the null finding resulted from an insensitive measure or a paradigm inherently incapable of priming.

text.text: The study was also powered to detect effects smaller than those typically reported within the incidental priming literature (e.g., DeCoster & Claypool, 2004; Kay et al., 2004; Weingarten et al., 2016), although smaller effects remain possible.
text.formatted: The study was also powered to detect effects smaller than those typically reported within the incidental priming literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">DeCoster & Claypool, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kay et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Weingarten et al., 2016)</ref>, although smaller effects remain possible.

text.text: The sensitivity analysis likewise did not alter the substantive interpretation.

Removing the single extreme Novel-condition trial increased both prime contrasts by a similar amount, raising the Home effect across the conventional significance threshold, while leaving the Work effect close to it.
However, since the removed observation contributed to the shared Novel baseline, rather than uniquely affecting the Home condition, this shift does not provide evidence for a Home-specific effect.
The precise size of the estimates is thus somewhat sensitive to this one trial, but the substantive pattern of two near-identical, same-direction contrasts remains unchanged.

This shared pattern is important because it does not match the category-specific divergence predicted by the semantic-affiliation account: Home and Work primes produced almost identical positive shifts despite the opposing directions predicted by H 1 and H 2 .
However, the present analysis alone cannot establish why the two familiar categories moved in the same direction.
The exploratory analyses therefore examined whether this pattern varied according to participants' pre-existing affiliations with home and work environments.
This analysis examined whether participants' relative affiliation with Home and Work environments moderated the effects of the object primes.
One interaction was in the predicted direction: the Home-versus-Novel effect was larger among Home-leaning than Balanced participants (b = 6.59, p = .033).
However, the evidence for affiliation-based moderation was limited.
The interaction was estimated from only five Home-leaning participants, so it was imprecise (95% CI [0.52, 12.66]).
It was also sensitive to how affiliation was operationalised.

Comparing Home-leaning participants with all other participants reduced the interaction to non-significance (b = 4.93, p = .062), whereas treating affiliation as a continuous score retained the effect (p = .046).

Most importantly, because the four interactions were tested as a family, significance was judged against a Bonferroni-corrected threshold (α = .0125; Field, 2024), which this interaction (p = .033) did not meet.
More tellingly, the interaction may reflect lower ratings following Novel primes among Homeleaning participants rather than greater responsiveness to the Home primes.

Home-leaning participants tended to rate Novel-primed faces lower than Balanced participants (b = -6.87, p = .058); because the Home effect is measured relative to the Novel condition, this lower baseline likely inflated the apparent interaction.

As Figure 6 shows, Novel-prime ratings generally fell below those following both Home and Work primes across the facetrustworthiness range, a pattern more consistent with a depressed Novel baseline than with a Home-specific increase, which further limits the support the interaction provides for an affiliation-based interpretation.
text.formatted: As Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">6</ref> shows, Novel-prime ratings generally fell below those following both Home and Work primes across the facetrustworthiness range, a pattern more consistent with a depressed Novel baseline than with a Home-specific increase, which further limits the support the interaction provides for an affiliation-based interpretation.

text.text: The source of this lower baseline is itself uncertain.
One possibility the design cannot rule out is that the affiliation measures capture broader dispositional differences rather than the categoryspecific valences they were intended to assess.

Pre-existing dispositions can influence how priming is expressed (Neuberg, 1988), and Home-and Work-leaning individuals may differ in related traits such as introversion and extraversion, which have been linked to variation in trustworthiness judgements (Evans & Revelle, 2008; Freitag & Bauer, 2016).
text.formatted: Pre-existing dispositions can influence how priming is expressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Neuberg, 1988)</ref>, and Home-and Work-leaning individuals may differ in related traits such as introversion and extraversion, which have been linked to variation in trustworthiness judgements <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Evans & Revelle, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Freitag & Bauer, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a more work-oriented, socially exposed (extraverted) disposition might be associated with more uniform trust judgements, whereas a more Home-oriented (introverted) disposition might be associated with lower baseline trust, which a Home prime may briefly offset.
This could explain why Home-leaning participants rated Novel-primed faces as less trustworthy than Work-leaning participants did, and why the Home primes briefly offset that difference.
No personality measure was collected, however, so this explanation remains speculative.
Taken together, the Home × Home-leaning interaction is best regarded as suggestive rather than robust evidence of affiliation-based moderation.
The data cannot distinguish a genuine but underpowered moderation from a baseline difference within the small Home-leaning subgroup.

This uncertainty motivated the final exploratory analysis, which examined whether a more direct index of exposure to work environments (self-reported workplace experience) similarly moderated the prime effects.

Work experience did not predict trustworthiness ratings or moderate either prime effect, providing no evidence in support for the accessibility prediction drawn from the situated inference model (Loersch & Payne, 2011), a finding that was unchanged in the sensitivity analysis.
text.formatted: Work experience did not predict trustworthiness ratings or moderate either prime effect, providing no evidence in support for the accessibility prediction drawn from the situated inference model <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>, a finding that was unchanged in the sensitivity analysis.

text.text: This null should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously: because work experience varies only between participants, moderation is estimated from just 28 individuals rather than the full trial set, and the confidence interval for the Work prime interaction (b = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.09]) reflects this imprecision.

The interval is consistent with effects ranging from a small negative to a small positive association; across the full 0 to 100 work experience scale, its upper bound corresponds to a ~9-point difference in trustworthiness ratings, while the point estimate corresponds to ~2 points.

The predicted interaction, whereby greater work exposure would strengthen the Work prime effect, was also the weaker and non-significant of the two, providing no support for this specific prediction of the accessibility account.
The primary interpretation therefore remains unchanged.
With the three analyses now considered individually, their combined implications can be drawn together.

Across the three analyses, the central interpretive challenge is that Home and Work primes produced similarly sized increases in trustworthiness ratings, rather than the opposing effects predicted by H 1 and H 2 .
The affiliation subgroup showed only limited, non-robust moderation, and work experience added none.
The pattern is therefore best described as two weak, samedirection effects of familiar object categories, not the category-specific divergence the semantic-affiliation account predicts.
One explanation is that the effect reflects familiarity rather than category-specific meaning.

Home and Work objects were familiar whereas Novel objects were not, and the processing fluency of familiarity can raise evaluations independently of a stimulus's specific content (Reber et al., 2004; Zajonc, 1968); on this account Home and Work resemble each other because both were familiar, not because they activated distinct trust-related representations.
text.formatted: Home and Work objects were familiar whereas Novel objects were not, and the processing fluency of familiarity can raise evaluations independently of a stimulus's specific content <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Reber et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Zajonc, 1968)</ref>; on this account Home and Work resemble each other because both were familiar, not because they activated distinct trust-related representations.

text.text: Equally, because the Novel objects lacked real-world referents, the same pattern could reflect these unfamiliar objects mildly depressing trust rather than the familiar categories raising it; either reading locates the effect in familiarity rather than social-category content.
A second possibility is that Home and Work objects are less psychologically opposed than originally assumed.

Both may evoke trust-relevant associations, or broader meanings acquired through their connections with people, activities, and social contexts (Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981; Dant, 1999; Nippert-Eng, 1996).
text.formatted: Both may evoke trust-relevant associations, or broader meanings acquired through their connections with people, activities, and social contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Csikszentmihalyi & Rochberg-Halton, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Dant, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Nippert-Eng, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: A third possibility is that object-evoked meanings were not readily applied to the trustworthiness judgement.

Priming effects on social judgement are generally modest and depend on conditions that allow activated information to bear on the target (Cesario, 2014; DeCoster & Claypool, 2004; Loersch & Payne, 2011), and here participants judged the face after only incidental exposure to an object, with multiple prime categories presented per participant further limiting how far any one meaning remained accessible.
text.formatted: Priming effects on social judgement are generally modest and depend on conditions that allow activated information to bear on the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Cesario, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">DeCoster & Claypool, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>, and here participants judged the face after only incidental exposure to an object, with multiple prime categories presented per participant further limiting how far any one meaning remained accessible.

text.text: The face itself also provided a strong cue to trustworthiness: normative facial trustworthiness shifted ratings across much of the response range, whereas the prime effects were only around two points.
The relatively small size of the prime effects therefore suggests that any object-evoked meaning may have had little scope to shift judgements that were already strongly determined by the facial cue.
These explanations are not mutually exclusive.
Familiarity may have conferred a general evaluative advantage on both familiar categories, while any category-specific meanings overlapped or transferred only weakly to the face.

Given that prime activation was not independently verified, the findings offer limited support for the semantic-affiliation account and cannot determine whether the absence of divergence reflects a general familiarity effect, overlapping category meanings, or a failure of object-evoked meaning to influence the target judgement.

On the practical question raised at the outset, the present data therefore give no reason to treat incidental object cues as a meaningful source of bias in everyday trustworthiness judgements, although they do not exclude effects under conditions in which object meaning is more directly relevant to the judgement being made.
These competing interpretations cannot be conclusively separated because several features of the design were not independently established.

The most consequential is the absence of a manipulation check confirming that the object categories activated their intended constructs; as a result, the null divergence is compatible with both successful activation that did not influence judgement and a failure of activation at the outset.

However, embedding such a check in the main experiment would be problematic, since revealing the Home-Work distinction risks disclosing the manipulation's purpose and thereby increasing demand characteristics, to which priming effects are sensitive (Bargh & Chartrand, 2000).
text.formatted: However, embedding such a check in the main experiment would be problematic, since revealing the Home-Work distinction risks disclosing the manipulation's purpose and thereby increasing demand characteristics, to which priming effects are sensitive <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bargh & Chartrand, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: A stronger approach would validate the prime categories in a separate sample, using measures such as lexical decision or word completion, so that failures of construct activation can be distinguished from failures to apply an activated construct to the target judgement.
A second limitation concerns how the object primes were integrated into the task.
Familiarity was confounded with category, since Home and Work objects were familiar, whereas Novel objects were not.
Consequently, higher ratings following the familiar categories cannot be unambiguously attributed to category-specific meaning rather than familiarity.
More importantly, the objects were presented incidentally and were not integrated into the trustworthiness judgement in a task-relevant way.
This may have limited the extent to which any object-evoked meaning was brought to bear on the subsequent social judgement.
Materialpriming studies reporting robust effects, such as Kay et al. (2004), instead embed objects within the context of the decision itself, increasing their relevance to the judgement being made.
text.formatted: Materialpriming studies reporting robust effects, such as <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kay et al. (2004)</ref>, instead embed objects within the context of the decision itself, increasing their relevance to the judgement being made.

text.text: Future research should therefore include a familiar but trust-irrelevant control category to separate familiarity from category meaning and should examine whether integrating object primes more directly into the judgement context produces stronger transfer to the social judgement (Loersch & Payne, 2011).
text.formatted: Future research should therefore include a familiar but trust-irrelevant control category to separate familiarity from category meaning and should examine whether integrating object primes more directly into the judgement context produces stronger transfer to the social judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Loersch & Payne, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: A third limitation is the study's limited treatment of individual differences relevant to trustworthiness judgement.
The exploratory affiliation analysis suggests that participant characteristics may contribute to variation in these judgements.
However, the measured affiliations may themselves index broader dispositions, such as introversion and extraversion.
Relatedly, a small number of participants reported to the experimenter that they were autistic and found everyday trustworthiness judgements difficult.
This represents potentially relevant unmodelled variation, given that autism has been associated with atypical facial trustworthiness evaluation (Adolphs et al., 2001; Forgeot d'Arc et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This represents potentially relevant unmodelled variation, given that autism has been associated with atypical facial trustworthiness evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adolphs et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Forgeot d'Arc et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These participants were nevertheless retained, as autism was not an exclusion criterion.
Furthermore, since the data were anonymised at collection, these verbal reports could not be linked to individual data records, and their influence on the results therefore cannot be assessed.

Future research should therefore measure theoretically relevant individual differences directly, allowing variation in social-cognitive processing to be modelled rather than inferred from subgroup patterns or addressed retrospectively.

Finally, the exploratory moderation analyses were limited by small subgroup sizes and low statistical power; therefore, the observed interactions should be considered tentative rather than robust evidence of individual-difference moderation.
A larger, preregistered replication specifically designed to detect interactions would provide a more rigorous test.
Where supported by the design, participant-level random slopes should be incorporated to model variation across individuals and conditions (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Where supported by the design, participant-level random slopes should be incorporated to model variation across individuals and conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, employing a broader stimulus set and recruiting a more diverse sample would help determine whether the observed pattern generalises beyond the current objects, faces, and predominantly young participants.
This study found no reliable evidence that incidental exposure to Home or Work objects altered trustworthiness judgements of unfamiliar faces under the conditions tested.

Although both familiar categories produced small, same-direction increases relative to Novel objects, neither effect was reliably distinguishable from zero, and the exploratory affiliation effect did not provide robust evidence of individual-difference moderation.
The findings therefore do not support the predicted category-specific divergence between Home and Work primes, but they also do not establish that everyday objects cannot influence social perception.
Instead, they indicate that any influence of object-related meaning on social judgement may be sensitive to how that meaning is activated and brought to bear on the target.

Further research should therefore establish whether the intended prime constructs are activated, separate familiarity from category meaning, and test object cues under conditions more conducive to transfer to interpersonal judgement.
This report presents all data collected for this study.

All conditions, measures and exclusions are reported, including the three affiliation probes administered at the end of the session and the two participants excluded for non-response, with one exception: a suspicion probe and an optional free-text comment were also collected at the end of the session but were not analysed.
Responses to the suspicion probe are included in the shared data; the free-text comments are not shared, to protect participants' confidentiality.

As the exploratory models share this random structure and the same 1,217 observations, the random-effect checks were conducted for the primary model and taken to generalise to both exploratory models.

The outlier trial was the single largest positive residual in the analysis, a Novel primed face at the lowest normative trust level (-3) that the participant nonetheless rated 68 on the 0 to 100 scale, far above the low value the model predicted for so untrustworthy a face.

Nonetheless, all trials were retained in the primary analysis; the single trial exceeding the threshold was a Novel-condition rating, so removing it would shift the shared baseline rather than isolate a prime-specific effect.

To confirm the conclusions did not depend on it, the model was nonetheless re-estimated with it removed to assess whether the outlier influenced the model (standardised residual = 3.40, |z| > 3.29; n = 1,216 trials).

Group-Based Interaction

As the Home prime × Home-leaning interaction was the only term to reach significance, it was re-estimated in isolation, with participants classed as Home-leaning (n = 5) versus all other participants (n = 23) and a single prime-by-group interaction retained.
The interaction was reduced and no longer significant, b = 4.93, SE = 2.64, t(1177.30) = 1.87, 95% CI [-0.25, 10.11], p = .062 with the interval now including zero.

Face-trust level remained strongly predictive, b = 4.61, 95% CI [4.15, 5.07], p < .001, and the variance components were essentially unchanged (participant 29.60, p = .003; face identity 21.53, p = .068; residual 271.03); the model converged without boundary estimates, marginal R² = .219 and conditional R² = .343.

Affiliation as a Continuous Moderator

The moderation observed in the profile-group model was re-examined with the Home-minus-Work affiliation difference entered as a continuous predictor interacting with the prime contrasts, avoiding the information loss associated with dividing participants into three groups using a fixed cut-off (all 1,217 trials; N = 28).

The Home prime × affiliation interaction was positive and reached conventional significance, b = 0.095, 95% CI [0.002, 0.189], p = .046, indicating that the Home-versus-Novel prime effect increased by ~0.10 rating points for each one-point increase in Home-leaning affiliation.
The Work prime × affiliation interaction was not significant, b = 0.063, 95% CI [-0.029, 0.156], p = .181, providing no evidence that Home-Work affiliation altered the effect of the Work prime.

The affiliation main effect was nonsignificant, b = -0.08, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.03], p = .134, as were both prime contrasts at a balanced affiliation score (Home, b = 1.78, 95% CI [-0.53, 4.08], p = .130; Work, b = 1.53, 95% CI [-0.74, 3.81], p = .186); thus, there was no evidence of a main effect of affiliation or of either prime contrasts.
This model did not converge; SPSS reported that iteration terminated without achieving convergence and that the validity of the fit was therefore uncertain.

Consistent with this, the Work-prime slope variance was estimated at the zero boundary (0.00), and the Homeprime slope variance was effectively unidentified, its 95% CI spanning from near zero to over 1.6 million (variance = 1.12, SE = 8.10, 95% CI [7.75, 1624165.05], p = .890).

The data therefore could not support by-participant random slopes for prime, consistent with the small number of trials per condition per participant and empirically supporting the random-intercept structure used throughout (Matuschek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The data therefore could not support by-participant random slopes for prime, consistent with the small number of trials per condition per participant and empirically supporting the random-intercept structure used throughout <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Since the model did not converge its estimates cannot be interpreted; although the interaction remained nominally close to the threshold (b = 6.68, p = .039), no weight can be placed on this value.
The interaction's robustness to a random-slope specification therefore could not be established, reinforcing the conclusion that it is best treated as a fragile, exploratory result.
